answer: The authors expect the vertex frequencies in short random walks to follow a power-law distribution when the graph has a highly skewed degree distribution, so that a few high-degree vertices are visited much more often than the rest. They draw an analogy to natural language by comparing this to Zipf’s law: just as a small number of words occur very frequently while most words are rare, a small number of vertices dominate the walk counts while most vertices appear infrequently.
confidence_reasoning: This matches the standard interpretation of random-walk visitation frequencies on scale-free or heavy-tailed graphs and the common Zipf’s-law analogy from language, though the exact wording may vary by source.
